title: Upper-arm length did not improve cross-cycle FVC prediction beyond flexible standard anthropometry
abstract: Upper-arm length could encode body proportions not captured by standing height, but whether that information improves held-out lung-volume prediction is uncertain. We fixed a one-term extension before testing its association: add measured upper-arm length to an empirical FVC model using age, sex, height, BMI, waist, smoking and self-reported race/ethnicity. We fitted NHANES 2007–2008 adults (n=3,749) and applied the frozen models to the separately recruited 2009–2010 dataset (n=4,171). Target RMSE was 518.992 mL without and 519.032 mL with the arm term. Baseline-minus-augmented RMSE was −0.040 mL (target stratified-PSU bootstrap 95% interval −0.566 to +0.457; source-and-target refit interval −0.965 to +0.470). Source five-fold out-of-fold gain was +0.137 mL. Survey weighting, stronger anthropometric flexibility and other sensitivity tests did not show a consistent benefit. This is a scoped negative predictive result, not proof that body proportions contain no physiological information or an equivalence study. Independent-programme validation was not performed.
